newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Japan economic mantras-clues or confusion?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Japan economic mantras-clues or confusion?.

text.p: Comments by Japanese economic policy makers can be contradictory, ambiguous or deadly dull, and some cynics dismiss most of them as meaningless.
Others, however, say that ignoring the steady stream of official remarks can be risky.

"Sometimes comments do tell you about policy. It's like pornography. You can't define it, but you know it when you see it," said one foreign economist. "There's no way to define when a statement has meaning, but when it does, it's pretty clear."

Given how often the authorities get to air their views at regular briefings, business conventions, parliamentary hearings and the twice-weekly news conferences that follow cabinet meetings, it's perhaps not surprising some phrases are echoed with mantra-like monotony.
CRACKING THE CODE

The meaning of the mantra can be crystal clear to those in the know, but to others, officials may seem to be speaking in tongues. Take a phrase commonly uttered these days by Japan's chief central banker, Yasuo Matsushita: "Japan will manage the economy to ensure recovery." Not very surprising, one might think, and not particularly meaningful either.

The comment, however, is seen typically as code for assurances that the Bank of Japan will keep its hyper-easy credit policy in place, despite the scope for higher interest rates ostensibly implied by Matsushita's equally frequent insistence that Japan's economic recovery is "getting firmer."
Other phrases may be mere fluff. Asked recently what he meant by "balanced economic management," Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka confessed the term was "political jargon."
Whether Japanese economic statements are tougher to interpret than comments by policy makers elsewhere is an open question.
"(U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan) Greenspan used the term 'irrational exuberance.' He's not going to come out and say, 'the stock market is over-bought'," said another economist.

Greenspan, whose December warning about "irrational exuberance" in financial markets was a red flag to Wall Street, has himself said that he was well-schooled in the central bankers' art of being both "cryptic" and "incomprehensible."
SO WHAT ELSE IS NEW?
Sifting through the latest in a string of Japanese pronouncements to find what's new can sometimes be daunting.

Phrases chosen to describe the state of the economy tend to be repeated for months on end until government planners judge that a new phase has begun and pluck up the courage to go public with their assessment.
Last November, for example, the government's Economic Planning Agency (EPA) took what it dubbed a "half-step forward" in assessing the economy, merely by omitting a few words.

The EPA, which since February last year had said Japan's economy was "recovering gradually despite some weakness," kept its by-then familiar reference to a gradual improvement but deleted the nagging phrase "there are some worrisome aspects." The "gradual recovery" refrain itself had replaced a diagnosis of the economy as "stalled," successor to the EPA's earlier rather eye-catching claim that the economy was "crawling along the bottom."
CLUES TO CURRENCY COMFORT LEVELS
Financial markets regard official mantra as providing clues on official comfort levels with currency rates, possible central bank intervention and potential credit policy shifts.

Markets already jittery over possible Bank of Japan intervention to prop up the faltering yen got a fresh jolt earlier this month, when Mitsuzuka twinned an already familiar threat to act against "excessive" currency moves with a comment that recent moves were, in fact, "overdone."

Some market pundits, however, were loath to put much stock in the remarks until they heard them uttered by senior finance ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara, whose ability to sway currency markets has earned him the sobriquet "Mr Yen."
"The market tends to think that Mitsuzuka is not really in charge," said the foreign economist.
CREDIBILTY CONTRAST

The tendency to wonder whether Japan's finance minister means what he says, or says what Japan means, contrasts with the credibility accorded to comments by his U.S. counterpart, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, several analysts said.
"If Rubin says something or doesn't say something, it's meaningful. If Mitsuzuka does it, it may be because he misread the script," the second economist said.
Rubin, a former investment banker, appears to relish his ability to keep markets guessing, some analysts said.
"He seems to delight in keeping people off balance," the foreign economist said. "He telegraphs changes (in stance) but then says nothing has changed."
REAL POLITICS, NOT ECONOMIC REALITY

Economists trying to diagnose the health of Japan's economy, however, take official mantra with a hefty dose of salt. "The government may have political incentives to make certain statements that may not coincide with economic reality," said the foreign economist.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, for example, has made cutting Japan's big budget deficit a policy priority, so he is unlikely to want officials worrying aloud about the impact of higher taxes and less government spending.
Hence, some economists say, the constant string of recent assurances that the recovery may slow in the early part of the new business year but that all will be rosy later.
SHORTAGE OF TIMELY DATA

Financial markets everywhere, of course, are obsessed with analysing words spoken by high-profile policy makers like Greenspan and Rubin. Japan, however, may be even more inclined to pore over official remarks, given the relative lack of timely economic data, some economists said.

"In Japan, the amount of superficial scrutiny is much more intense than elsewhere," said one European economist. "In America, they cling to the data release schedule, which is much more intense. Analysis focuses on facts, not words. In Japan, the data is all lagging, and there are so many more words."
MAVERICKS CAN MISLEAD
Markets can at times be thrown off track temporarily by politicians speaking out of turn on touchy topics.
Cabinet minister Kabun Muto gave the dollar a brief boost against the yen last week when he told reporters that any "artifical" attempt to check further yen falls might well fail.

Muto, whose Management and Coordination Agency is hardly a top economic ministry, also said there was nothing wrong with the dollar moving above 125 yen but that Japan should raise its official discount rate to discourage capital outflows.
Shortly afterwards, a finance ministry official said Muto's remarks did "not reflect the official policy of the Japanese government" and the dollar fell back a bit.
"You're always going to have the problem of some guy coming out of left field. Then you have to figure out where he stands in the policy pecking order," the European economist said.
